records.quote: Key parameters affecting the smoke properties of the smoke produced here are the low-gravity condition, the convective flow past the heated wire, the wire temperature, and the aging time.
records.derivation: The source term is 'low-gravity', mapped to the controlled value microgravity. The sentence is about the smoke produced in the SAMER flight tests (section D of the report, an excerpt of the authors' SAME-2 paper; the same sentence is in Appendix F, page=82). '*' means the flight tests of the Appendix A test matrix (pages 31-49), which are the tests in the PSI tables. The post-flight ground tests are separate records (R3, R4). NOT A FLAME: a wire heated the samples below the ignition point and the smoke came from pyrolysis. Appendix F page=72: 'were heated to temperatures below the ignition point'. Page=8: 'As the samples are heated by the wire, chemical bonds are broken and gaseous products are released via pyrolysis.' Not used as gravity evidence: the PSI label projectType 'Microgravity Investigation' and the platform statements ('on orbit', 'uploaded to ISS').

records.quote: Similar to the original SAME investigation, the primary objective of the SAME-R investigation was to quantify the sizes that the liquid smoke particulate achieves in low gravity and to relate the droplet size distribution to the smoke generation and smoke transport conditions in the experiment.
records.derivation: This sentence states an objective, not the condition of the tests, so it only supports R1. 'liquid smoke particulate' and 'droplet' describe the smoke aerosol, not the sample; see R5 and R6 for the sample phase.

records.test_id: post-flight ground TEM tests (no NASA test id; not in the Appendix A flight test matrix)
records.quote: As a part of SAMER effort, three major post–flight ground tests were performed: the SAMER apparatus flow tests to obtain accurate dilution ratio data, the TEM tests to obtain the 1-g counterpart of TEM samples and a batch of SMPS tests to examine the validity of the lognormal distribution assumption of aerosol particle size for the tested materials.
records.derivation: The sentence states '1-g' only for the ground TEM tests. Page=2 (Introduction) adds that those tests 'were conducted under exactly the same conditions as those for the SAMER flight tests so that the gravity effects on the TEM samples can be identified.' These are ground comparison tests. Do not attach them to any flight-test row of the PSI tables.

records.test_id: post-flight ground SMPS drum tests (no NASA test id; not in the Appendix A flight test matrix)
records.quote: In order to assess whether the size distribution of the smoke is lognormal, detailed particle size distributions were measured with a reference instrument. This cannot be accomplished in low gravity, so this investigation was performed with the ground-based engineering SAME hardware which is identical to the setup on the ISS, incorporating the flight aerosol instruments which had been returned to earth.
records.derivation: The sentence never writes '1-g' or 'normal gravity'. It says the measurement could not be done in low gravity, so it was done with ground-based hardware. Treating that as normal gravity is an inference, hence 'ambiguous'. Ground tests only; not flight-test rows.

records.quote: For part 2, only about the half of the wire surface is exposed to air. The other half is in contact with the solid sample.
records.derivation: The sentence comes from the section 'SAME heater temperature modeling' (pages 26-28), which page=26 applies to both investigations ('For SAME and SAMER, during a test, the software controls the temperature via the resistance of heating wire.'). The samples were heated, not burned (see R1 derivation and R6). Caveat for the auditor: page=4 (repeated on page=78) lists '6 materials' that include 'dibutyl-phthalate deposited on a porous wick', a liquid on a wick. But page=2 says Pyrell 'was introduced to replace DBP samples', and the Appendix A test matrix (pages 31-49) lists only Silicone, Lampwick, Teflon, Kapton and Pyrell. No SAME-R test in the matrix uses DBP. Not resolved further here.

records.value_original: Teflon, Kapton, cotton, silicone rubber and Pyrell
records.quote: Five different materials representative of those found in spacecraft (Teflon, Kapton, cotton, silicone rubber and Pyrell) were heated to temperatures below the ignition point with conditions controlled to provide repeatable sample surface temperatures and air flow.
records.derivation: Inferred from the material names: all five are solid materials (Teflon, Kapton, cotton/lamp wick, silicone rubber, and Pyrell, which the record approach calls 'an intumescent fire-retardant foam'). The same sentence says the samples were heated below the ignition point. They were pyrolyzed, not burned with a flame. Source: Appendix F abstract (SAME-2 paper = SAME-R).
PSI field label (not a sentence); corroborated by R8.

records.quote: Six re-assembled Thermal Precipitators, each having 12 TEM grids in it, were uploaded to ISS for SAMER.
records.derivation: Also on page=3: 'In addition to those preloaded carousels, thirty loose samples were also uploaded to ISS.'

records.quote: An unfortunate side effect was that approximately half the smoke was lost from the system because it diffused out of the inlet into the MSG volume.
records.derivation: The sentence is about the SAME-R zero-flow tests. Smoke escaping 'into the MSG volume' implies the hardware ran inside the MSG. The abbreviation is expanded as 'Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG)' on page=2. Appendix F page=75 says it directly for SAME (both flights): 'The system was installed in the Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG), an ISS facility...'. That page's text layer is fragmented into columns, so it was not used as the quote.

records.quote: SAMER is an extension or continuation of Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME), which was conducted in the Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG) onboard the International Space Station (ISS) from September 9 to October 5, 2007.
records.derivation: The sentence states the MSG location for the original SAME flight (2007), not for SAME-R. Applying it to SAME-R rests on page=3: 'SAME-R utilized the SAME hardware already on orbit with reloaded sample carousels, 30 extra loose samples, rebuilt thermal precipitators and refilled alcohol cartridge for P-trak use.'

records.quote: The test conditions included multiple sample temperatures and air flow rates.
records.derivation: air: oxygen balanced mainly by nitrogen. The gas past the heated sample is air, including the no-flow cases. Appendix F page=72 says 'The air flow past the sample during the heating period ranged from quiescent to 8 cm/s.' The air composition is not stated. Do NOT use the N2 on page=25 ('the aerosol stream was diluted with the N2 gas provided by the ISS'). That N2 dilutes the smoke sample downstream for the P-Trak and DustTrak instruments; it is not the gas around the sample.

record text (all sections); Final Report pages 1-89; docx sample-description tables. The gas is named 'air' (page=4, page=72), but no oxygen concentration is stated.

record text (all sections); Final Report pages 1-89; docx sample-description tables. Only sample/wire heating temperatures appear (e.g. Table 2, page=16, 225.3-574.3 °C), plus 'room temperature' with no value (page=26). Neither is the ambient gas temperature.

lineage: SAME-R reflew the SAME hardware already on the ISS and uses the SAME final report for hardware and method. Record section=approach: 'SAME-R utilized the SAME hardware used on-orbit.' Final Report page=3: 'Since the SAMER project is a re-flight of SAME, the hardware, the project approach, the principle of moment method, post flight data analysis and uncertainty analysis will not be repeated in this report.' Appendix F (page=74) uses 'SAME' for statements covering both flights. The shared-instrument link between SAME and DAFT given in the task is not stated anywhere in the PSI-101 sources read: DAFT is not mentioned, so it remains unverified here. Note: record section=experimentHardware reads 'Comparitive Soot Diagnostic Hardware; Refer to final report'. That names the earlier CSD experiment (cited as a predecessor in Appendix F, page=73), which conflicts with the approach and the report, both of which say the SAME hardware was used.
